''Tillandsia bracteata'' Vell. }} '''''Aechmea fasciata''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Bromeliaceae]] family.{{cite web|url= https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:121640-1|title= Aechmea fasciata (Lindl.) Baker|author=|date=n.d.|website=Plants of the World Online|publisher=The Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|access-date=July 22, 2020}} It is commonly called the '''silver vase''' or '''urn plant''' and is native to Brazil. This plant is probably the best known species in this [[genus]], and it is often grown as a [[houseplant]] in [[temperateness|temperate]] areas. ==Description== The plant grows slowly, reaching {{convert|30|-|90|cm|0|abbr=on}} in height, with a spread of up to {{convert|60|cm|0|abbr=on}}. It has elliptic–oval-shaped leaves {{convert|45|-|90|cm|0|abbr=on}} long and arranged in a [[basal rosette]] pattern. The robust leaves have armored edges (like all members of the Bromelioideae). The leaf sheath is {{convert|9|-|10|cm|0|abbr=on}} wide. The {{convert|6|cm|0|abbr=on}} wide [[leaf blade]] is rounded at the end, but with a 4 mm long spine tip. Large amounts of water often collect in the leaf funnels. In their natural habitat, many of the funnels contain small [[biotope]]s with several animal species, as well as [[algae]] and aquatic plants. The leaves have whitish sucking scales ([[trichomes]]) on the upper and lower surfaces. These are distributed differently depending on the variety: they can cover the entire surface, or there are transverse bands with or without scales, which results in an interesting leaf pattern. There are also varieties with yellowish longitudinal lines ([[variegation]]).{{cite report |url=https://hort.ifas.ufl.edu/database/documents/pdf/shrub_fact_sheets/aecfasa.pdf |title=''Aechmea fasciata'' |last=Gilman |first=Edward F. |date=October 1999 |publisher=University of Florida Cooperative Extension Service |accessdate=2009-11-09}} ===Inflorescence=== [[File:At Jardín de Aclimatación de La Orotava 2023 054.jpg|thumb|left|In flower]] The [[inflorescence]] stem has a diameter of 1 cm and a length of {{convert|30|-|40|cm|0|abbr=on}}. The long-lasting, capitate-pyramidal inflorescences, branched at the base and simple at the apex, are composed of spike-like inflorescences. The inflorescences are borne on striking pink [[bract]]s with a spiny, toothed margin. The [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]], [[hermaphroditic]], three-[[petal]]ed flowers are about {{convert|3.5|cm|0|abbr=on}} long. The three asymmetrical, {{convert|1|cm|0|abbr=on}} long [[sepal]]s are fused into a short (2.5 mm) tube; they are pink, covered in white woolly scales and blunt at the end. The three {{convert|3|cm|0|abbr=on}} long petals are fused into a short tube. Two small scales on the petals ([[ligule]]s) form a characteristic that botanists use to distinguish them from other genera in the subfamily. The color of the petals is initially blue; as they wilt, they turn red at the top and white towards the base. There are two circles, each with three [[stamen]]s. Three [[carpel]]s are fused into an inferior [[ovary]], which is 5 to 6 mm in diameter and 6 to 8 mm long. ==Cultivation== [[File:Aechmea fasciata Lincoln Conservatory.JPG|thumb|left|Flower close-up]] ''Aechmea fasciata'' requires partial shade to bright indirect light, and can handle brief periods of early morning sunlight, but should be shielded from the sun during the hottest parts of the day. Excessive sun exposure will cause burning on the foliage and dehydration of the plant; comparatively, reduced sunlight or darker conditions will prevent the plant's characteristic coloration and striping from developing fully, instead reverting to a deeper hue of pastel-green/teal-blue in an effort to [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesize]] effectively in the shade. Less bright indirect light will also limit flowering. As with all bromeliads and [[epiphyte]]s, ''Aechmea fasciata'' requires adequate airflow around the entire plant to stay fresh. Over time, the plant’s roots will adhere to the surface provided, and the plant will form a small colony. The gardener simply keeps the "cup" or funnels filled with water. This method of cultivation is mostly executed successfully outdoors, rather than indoors, and is best-achieved in appropriate climates, especially maritime or seaside locations where the bromeliad may absorb moisture via [[fog]] and [[marine layer]]. ===Growth media=== [[File:Aechmea fasciata kz1.JPG|thumb|Growing in clumps in natural [[mulch]]]] A well-drained, but moisture-retentive soil, is recommended, including prepared orchid or cactus and succulent soil mixes. It is often recommended for gardeners to add additional inert materials, such as [[pumice]], [[perlite]], [[Volcanic rock|lava rock]], or [[vermiculite]], as well as optional chunks of orchid bark or coconut chips/husks. [[Root rot]] can be a problem in potted indoor plants, if the soil is too moist or does not contain enough inert drainage material. Potted bromeliads, alternatively, will thrive in a medium of pure [[sphagnum]] moss, as this substrate absorbs water effectively while remaining porous enough to dry and let the roots breathe. The rosette "cups", formed by the leaves, should be kept filled with water, although adequate evaporation is necessary to prevent crown rot in indoor specimens. Bromeliads can also be grown epiphytically, or mounted, with dried [[Sphagnum|sphagnum moss]] tied around their roots, with the entire plant then tied (with string or wire) to a board, cork bark, driftwood, or even a living tree branch, among other choices. The plants may also be attached using [[Cyanoacrylate|superglue]], [[Hot-melt adhesive|hot glue]], or [[Silicone rubber|silicone sealant]] (preferably labeled as pond- and fish-safe, which is commonly used with plants). ===Propagation=== Propagation is from [[Offset (botany)|side-shoots]] ("pups") that naturally develop around the base of the main rosette.{{cite book |last1=Chiusoli |first1=Alessandro |last2=Boriani |first2=Luisa Maria |title=Simon & Schuster's guide to houseplants |date=1986 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |location=New York |isbn=0671631314}} A sharp, [[Isopropyl alcohol|alcohol]]-sterilized knife may be used to [[Division (horticulture)|remove plantlets]] that have grown to several inches in height, cutting as close to the base as possible to retain any young roots that have formed. Removal of pups that are too small or underdeveloped often simply results in their [[desiccation]] and death. ===Pests=== [[Scale insect]]s may be attracted to the tight spaces between leaves, and [[mosquito]]s will sometimes (though rarely) breed in the pools of water that are accumulated in the plant—in outdoor specimens, specifically. Hence, regular flushing with water is recommended if rain does not regularly occur. ==Toxicity== ''Aechmea fasciata'', while not lethally [[List of poisonous plants|poisonous]], is listed in the [[Food and Drug Administration|FDA]] Poisonous Plant Database under the section "skin-irritating substances in plants". As bromeliads naturally produce the [[enzyme]] and alkaloid [[bromelain]]—commonly extracted from [[pineapple]]s (also a bromeliad) as a supplement and [[digestive enzyme]]—, skin contact with the plant's sharp, serrated leaf margins is known to cause [[Contact dermatitis|contact dermititis]], [[phytophotodermatitis]], and contact allergy; typical side effects are a mild, itchy sensation or redness.{{cite web|title=FDA Poisonous Plant Database|url=http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/plantox/detail.cfm?id=17611|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808102301/http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/plantox/detail.cfm?id=17611|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 8, 2014|website=U.S. Food and Drug Administration|accessdate=21 July 2014}} Therefore leather gloves are recommended when working with bromeliads, for example, arm-length or rose-pruning gloves.
